passages.original: Video igitur et curiosius et plenius agendum ab originibus usque ad profectus et excessus rei. Litterae ad hoc saeculares necessariae. De suis enim instrumentis saecularia probari necesse est. Quantulas attigi, credo sufficient. Si fuit aliqua Pandora, quam primam feminarum memorat Hesiodus, hoc primum caput coronatum est a Charitibus, cum ab omnibus muneraretur, unde Pandora. Nobis vero Moyses, propheticus, non poeticus pastor, principem feminam Evam facilius pudenda foliis quam tempora floribus incinctam describit.
passages.english: I see, then, that the matter must be treated both more carefully and more fully, from its origins right through to its developments and excesses. For this, secular literature is necessary, since secular things must be proved from their own documents. The little of it I have touched on will, I think, suffice. If there was ever a Pandora, whom Hesiod records as the first of women, hers was the first head crowned, by the Graces, when she was being presented with gifts by all [the gods], whence [the name] Pandora. But to us Moses, a shepherd who was a prophet, not a poet, describes the first woman, Eve, as girded about her private parts with leaves rather than about her temples with flowers.

passages.original: Nulla ergo Pandora. Sed et de mendacio erubescenda est coronae origo. Iam nunc et de veritatibus suis. Certe enim certos fuisse constat auctores rei vel illuminatores. Saturnum Pherecydes ante omnes refert coronatum, Iovem Diodorus post devictos Titanas hoc munere a ceteris honoratum. Dat et Priapo taenias idem, et Ariadnae sertum ex auro et Indicis gemmis, Vulcani ac post Liberi munus, postea sidus Iunoni vitem Callimachus induxit.
passages.english: There was, then, no Pandora. But the origin of the crown must also be blushed for on account of the lie. Now let us turn also to its truths [i.e. what is held as fact about it]. For it is certainly agreed that there were definite originators or promoters of the thing. Pherecydes reports that Saturn was crowned before all others; Diodorus, that Jupiter was honoured with this gift by the others after the Titans were defeated. The same [writer] gives fillets to Priapus as well, and to Ariadne a garland of gold and Indian gems, the gift of Vulcan and afterwards of Liber, later a constellation. Callimachus put a vine [wreath] on Juno.
passages.notes: The punctuation of the Ariadne/Juno clause is uncertain; 'postea sidus' may refer to the garland becoming a constellation.

passages.original: Ita et Argis signum eius palmite redimitum subiecto pedibus corio leonino insultantem ostentat novercam de exuviis utriusque privigni Hercules nunc populum capite praefert, nunc oleastrum, nunc apium. Habes tragoediam Cerberi. habes Pindarum atque Callimachum, qui et Apollinem memorat interfecto Delphyne dracone lauream induisse, qua supplicem. Erant enim supplices coronati apud veteres. Liberum, eundem apud Aegyptios Osirin, Harpocration industria hederatum argumentatur, quod hederae natura sit cerebrum ab heluco defensare.
passages.english: So also at Argos her statue, bound with a vine-shoot, with a lion's skin placed beneath her feet, displays the stepmother triumphing over the spoils of both her stepsons. Hercules wears on his head now poplar, now wild olive, now parsley. You have the tragedy of Cerberus; you have Pindar and Callimachus, who also records that Apollo, after killing the serpent Delphyne, put on laurel as a suppliant. For among the ancients suppliants were crowned. Harpocration argues that Liber, who among the Egyptians is the same as Osiris, was purposely wreathed with ivy, because it is the nature of ivy to protect the brain from drunken stupor.
passages.notes: 'Both stepsons' presumably Hercules and Liber (Bacchus). 'heluco' is obscure; taken as heavy-headedness from wine (cf. helluo).

passages.original: Hae enim erant pompae diaboli et angelorum eius, officia saeculi, honores, sollemnitates, popularitates, falsa vota, humana servitia, laudes vanae, gloriae turpes, et in omnibus istis idololatriae in solo quoque censu coronarum, quibus omnia ista redimita sunt. Praefabitur quidem Claudius etiam caelum sideribus apud Homeri carmina coronatum, certe a deo, certe homini; igitur et homo ipse a deo coronandus est. Ceterum a saeculo coronantur et lupanaria et latrinae et pistrinae et carcer et ludus et ipsa amphitheatra et ipsa spoliaria ipsaeque libitinae.
passages.english: For these were the pomps of the devil and his angels: the offices of the world, honours, festivals, courting of popularity, false vows, human servitudes, empty praises, shameful glories, and in all these, idolatry, even in the mere matter of crowns, with which all these things are wreathed. Claudius will indeed say in his preface that the heaven too is crowned with stars in the poems of Homer, surely by God, surely for man; therefore man himself also is to be crowned by God. But by the world are crowned brothels, and latrines, and bakehouses, and the prison, and the gladiatorial school, and the very amphitheatres, and the very stripping-rooms for the slain, and the very biers of the dead.
